extracted.intended_audience: American statesmen and the educated public (legislators, political philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative criteria for constitutions and republican governments, focusing on balance of powers, institutions (senates, assemblies, magistrates), and protections of individual and civic rights. Draws historical examples to justify institutional design choices for the United States and comparable polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of power among the one, the few, and the many
rubrics_metrics.description: Power within the state must be balanced among the one, the few, and the many; a mixed government 'partaking of the known forms' is the best safeguard against tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance is likened to three scales held by a third hand; if the balance is broken by mighty weights the state will run into one extreme. Historical examples (Sparta, Rome, Carthage, Athens) show that when the balance fails (Decemviri, Ephori, the four hundred, the thirty, Dominatio Plebis) tyranny follows. The balancing of powers should check the passions peculiar to each order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of the legislative, executive, and judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, executive, and judicial powers ought to be carefully separated and independent of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where these powers are carefully separated — as in the United States — 'the laws alone can govern.' Absence of distinct separation is observed in no one government surveyed, except England as a partial exception. Separation is necessary to enact and execute equal laws by common consent for the general interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal magistrate (a head) is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Every body politic requires a distinguished officer or principal magistrate (a 'head'); no society subsists without one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across republics one meets a chief under various names (stadtholder, doge, president, governor, king). The presence of such a head is natural and necessary; instituting governors is not justly censurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit senate/upper council to legislative function (avoid executive/judicial roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senates or 'little councils' should be confined to legislative power and not share executive or judicial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When senates are debarred from executive power and confined to the legislative, they have served as 'firm barriers' against encroachments of the crown and supporters of popular liberties. Conversely, admitting senates to executive/judicial functions tends to generate aristocratic ambition and a tyrannical oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies should be adequate, proportional, and equitable representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular assemblies (houses of representatives) should provide the most adequate, proportional, and equitable representation of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American assemblies are praised as the most adequate known; appointing a house (or houses) of representatives is defended as appropriate representation for the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly ascertained and publicly known limits of power for each party
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits of the powers deposited with each division (one, few, many) ought to be ascertained and generally known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to define limits produces continual struggles in a state about prerogative and liberty, leading to encroachments and eventually tyranny; public knowledge of boundaries helps preserve balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve trial by jury and other legal protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial by jury and related legal safeguards (e.g., habeas corpus) must be preserved as fundamental checks on power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trials by jury are 'preserved in all their glory' in the United States; habeas corpus 'in full force' is highlighted as a liberty-protecting institution. These legal protections are part of what enables laws to govern and restrains arbitrary power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of a standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance of a standing army is important for preserving the people's power and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises England's preservation of liberties by constantly refusing a standing army; standing armies empower rulers to curb the people and nobility at the expense of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hereditary titles, honours, or permanent orders of birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should not recognize hereditary titles, honours, offices, or distinctions that create a permanent nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In America 'there are no hereditary titles, honours, offices, or distinctions,' property is in citizens' hands, officials are chosen (often annually), and such arrangements sustain popular sovereignty and equality before law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free press as a safeguard of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A free press is an essential element of political liberty and public accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press is noted as 'the most free in the world' where other safeguards exist; freedom of the press is listed among the circumstances enabling laws alone to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of authority in a single assembly without adequate checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating all authority in a single assembly (collecting all authority into one center) risks overthrowing the balance of power unless adequate checks exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text debates Mr. Turgot's and Dr. Franklin's reputed opinions (single assembly vs. two assemblies). It warns that single, unchecked assemblies can overbalance and be easily disarmed or become dangerous; balancing mechanisms (e.g., a 'pointed rod' / counterweight) are necessary if power is concentrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect, participation, and humane treatment of the populace
rubrics_metrics.description: The people (populace) must be regarded as the principal support of the nation and treated with consideration, rights, and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degrading or debasing the populace ('fallen from all the rights of humanity') invites revolt and insurrection; their labour, taxes, and contributions merit better returns than scorn and disdain. Examples: misery can drive desperate insurrections (Ukraine). Enfranchisement and participation preserve stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional inventions to check particular passions of each order
rubrics_metrics.description: Create institutional contrivances (rotations, mixed selection methods, blended elections) to check the passions of the one, the few, and the many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across republics there are 'ingenious inventions'—mixing lot and choice, combining different bodies in elections, rotations of office—to prevent any order from being wholly influenced by a junta or becoming oligarchic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of administrative councils from experienced officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative or 'little' councils should be composed generally of those officers of state with the most experience and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such councils bear the principal burden of administration and often share in legislative, executive, and judicial authority; their composition affects the dynamics of ambition and the risk of aristocratic tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid aristocratic consolidation and manipulation of office rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent noble or patrician families from engineering rotations, contests, and selection methods that secure a perpetual oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrician families attempt to reduce a head's power and secure pre-eminence by rotation, blending lot and choice, and mixing bodies in elections; these measures often aim to preserve their privileges and can nonetheless create a tyrannical oligarchy if unchecked.
